lines.watchItem: Demand keeps running ahead of what the chain can build: the leading accelerator vendor guided next fiscal year to about 70 percent growth while saying customer forecasts implied roughly 140 percent, and TSMC says it still cannot meet demand while building about twenty plants at once. Wafer-start planning is exposed to how fast construction labour and tool deliveries let new lines come up, with tool demand now near 1.9 times the level projected nine months earlier.

Advanced-packaging allocation is again described as the binding limit on AI system availability, with lines quoted at roughly 52 to 78 weeks and capacity around 105,000 to 130,000 wafers a month by the fourth quarter. How much accelerator revenue the market can actually realise turns on that allocation more than on wafer starts.

Advanced-packaging capacity is pre-booked above 85 percent for 2026 and 2027, with one buyer holding roughly 60 percent and the top three more than 85 percent. That concentration means a single buyer trimming orders would leave slots that are hard to refill quickly.

A second packaging route is gathering real orders: Google has committed to more than three million units of Intel bridge packaging for delivery in 2028, Intel reports high yields and a growing backlog aimed at volume in 2027, and Intel holds about 14 percent of global 2.5D capacity against TSMC's roughly 70 percent. The route has its own limits, since its sole silicon-capacitor supplier is already fully booked.

The leading-node customer base is broadening from merchant accelerator vendors toward model builders and cloud in-house parts: OpenAI's first inference chip is built on a 3-nanometre process, Microsoft is reported to be negotiating capacity for upward of 300,000 of its own accelerators for 2027, and Broadcom guides this year's AI chip revenue to about $58 billion with a stated path to $230 billion in fiscal 2028. A third design house is also entering, with its first part in production in the fourth quarter of 2026.

Bargaining power on price is shifting toward whoever holds the scarce input rather than the chip designer: memory costs are pushing the leading vendor's gross margin from 75 percent toward a stated floor of 71 to 72 percent, it is raising system prices by more than 15 percent from early next year, and memory and flash costs are reported up over 300 percent year on year. Samsung has also lifted advanced contract chipmaking prices 10 to 15 percent on new orders.

Stacked memory competes for the same silicon and leaves no cushion: buffers at the two largest suppliers have fallen below ten days, the newest stacked memory is reported to consume about three times the wafer capacity of standard memory, and bit demand is expected to outgrow bit supply by more than ten percentage points next year. One supplier says it can serve only about half of what customers ask for.

Second-source and policy events are stacking up around the foundry position: Intel's foundry revenue grew 31 percent year over year with margins improving, Samsung holds about 7 percent of foundry revenue against TSMC's more than 70 percent and is in early talks to make a model builder's custom chip on a 2-nanometre process, and Washington is preparing chip tariffs that would reach finished servers with duty-free allowances sized to a company's United States fabrication investment.
